steps: Identify local (Nigerian) expenditure items: Nigerian labour = ₦60 million; locally manufactured materials = ₦80 million. Total local spend = 60 + 80 = ₦140 million.
Identify foreign expenditure items: imported equipment = ₦40 million; foreign services = ₦20 million. Total foreign spend = 40 + 20 = ₦60 million.
Verify total: 140 + 60 = ₦200 million. ✓
Calculate local content percentage: Local Content % = (Local spend / Total contract value) × 100 = (140 / 200) × 100 = 70 %.
Compare with the 65 % target: 70 % > 65 %, so the target is exceeded by 5 percentage points.

Comment. By maximising locally manufactured materials and Nigerian labour, the contractor retains ₦140 million within the domestic economy, supporting local jobs and industrial capacity in line with Nigeria's Local Content Act.
workedExamples.answer: Local content = 70 %, which exceeds the 65 % target. The contract complies with local content requirements.

workedExamples.title: Break-even analysis for an engineering start-up
workedExamples.problem: A recent engineering graduate sets up a solar photovoltaic installation business. Annual fixed costs (rent, salaries, insurance, loan repayment) total ₦500,000. The variable cost of each residential installation (panels, inverter, wiring, transport) is ₦80,000 per system, and each system is sold and installed for ₦150,000. How many installations must the business complete per year to break even, and what is the annual profit if 15 installations are completed?
steps: Calculate the contribution margin per installation: Contribution = Selling price − Variable cost = ₦150,000 − ₦80,000 = ₦70,000 per installation.
Apply the break-even formula: Break-even quantity = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit = ₦500,000 / ₦70,000 = 7.14 installations.
Since installations are whole units, round up: the business must complete at least 8 installations per year to cover all its costs.
Calculate profit at 15 installations: Profit = (Contribution per unit × Quantity) − Fixed costs = (70,000 × 15) − 500,000 = 1,050,000 − 500,000 = ₦550,000 per year.

Interpret. The business becomes profitable after the 8th installation. At 15 installations it earns ₦550,000 annually, demonstrating that small-scale engineering entrepreneurship in renewable energy can be commercially viable even at modest volumes.
workedExamples.answer: Break-even point = 8 installations per year. At 15 installations, annual profit = ₦550,000.

quiz.question: A 12-year infrastructure project has an initial cost of ₦80 million and generates uniform annual net benefits of ₦12 million. Using a discount rate of 10 %, PVIFA(10 %, 12) = 6.814. What is the project's NPV?
options: −₦80.0 million
−₦61.2 million
+₦1.77 million
+₦64.0 million
quiz.explanation: NPV = −80 + 12 × 6.814 = −80 + 81.77 = +₦1.77 million; the project is marginally viable.

quiz.question: Which phase of the engineering project life cycle is the correct stage to conduct a feasibility study?
options: Operation and maintenance
Procurement and construction
Conception and initiation
Decommissioning and disposal
quiz.explanation: A feasibility study belongs to the conception and initiation phase, when it is still inexpensive to abandon the project if it proves unviable.

quiz.question: A contractor spends ₦90 million locally and ₦60 million on foreign inputs on a ₦150 million project. What is the local content percentage, and does it meet a 55 % target?
options: 40 %; no, it falls short
55 %; yes, it exactly meets the target
60 %; yes, it exceeds the target
65 %; yes, it exceeds the target
quiz.explanation: Local content % = (90/150) × 100 = 60 %, which exceeds the 55 % target.

quiz.question: Technology transfer is considered fully successful only when:
options: The recipient country has paid all licensing fees to the originating country
Foreign experts are permanently stationed at the recipient facility
Local engineers can independently operate, maintain and improve the acquired technology
The technology has been patented in the recipient country's name
quiz.explanation: True technology transfer requires genuine absorption of knowledge so that local engineers no longer depend on the original supplier; payment or foreign presence alone does not achieve this.
